content: Anemia is a common factor that exacerbates postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The majority of deaths associated with PPH could be prevented through the use of prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labor and by providing appropriate treatment. Improving healthcare for women during childbirth to prevent and treat PPH is essential for achieving the health targets outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Approximately 99% of all maternal deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Efforts to prevent and reduce PPH-related morbidity and mortality can help address the significant inequities in maternal health globally. To support this, healthcare workers at all levels, particularly in LMICs, must have access to appropriate medications and training in relevant procedures. Additionally, healthcare providers, managers, policymakers, and other stakeholders require up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices, ultimately improving healthcare outcomes. In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) published 32 recommendations for the prevention and treatment of PPH, including a recommendation on the use of tranexamic acid (TXA) for PPH treatment. These recommendations were developed following WHO guideline development standards, which included synthesizing available research evidence, applying the GRADE methodology, and formulating recommendations through a panel of international experts. In 2017, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) on WHO maternal and perinatal health recommendations prioritized updating the existing WHO recommendation on TXA use for PPH treatment in response to new evidence. This updated recommendation supersedes the previous 2012 recommendation. At the time of the 2012 recommendation, there was no direct evidence on the effectiveness and safety of TXA for PPH treatment. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) conditionally recommended TXA use only when uterotonics failed to control bleeding or when bleeding was partially due to trauma. The WOMAN trial, a large randomized controlled trial, was conducted to examine the effects of early TXA administration on mortality, hysterectomy, and other morbidities in women with clinically diagnosed PPH. The trial has since concluded, and its primary findings were published in April 2017. Based on this new evidence, the Executive GSG prioritized updating the TXA recommendation for PPH treatment. As part of WHO’s normative work to support evidence-informed policies and practices, the Department of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) updated the recommendation on TXA use for PPH treatment. This updated recommendation provides a foundation for the sustainable global implementation of this intervention. The primary audience for this recommendation includes health professionals responsible for developing national and local health guidelines and protocols, particularly those related to PPH, as well as those directly providing care to women during labor and childbirth. This includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, maternal and child health program managers, and relevant staff in ministries of health across all settings. The recommendation is also relevant to professional societies involved in the care of pregnant women, non-governmental organizations promoting people-centered maternal care, and implementers of maternal and child health programs. The scope of the recommendation addresses the question: In women with PPH, does the administration of TXA for PPH treatment, compared to placebo, no treatment, or other treatments, improve outcomes? If so, what is the most appropriate period to administer TXA to improve outcomes? The affected population includes women experiencing PPH in low-, middle-, or high-income settings. The updated recommendation was developed using standardized operating procedures in accordance with the WHO handbook for guideline development. The process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing evidence, formulating the recommendation, and planning for dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updating of the recommendation. The WHO recommendation on TXA use for PPH treatment was identified as a high priority for updating in response to new evidence. The updating process involved five main groups, each with specific roles: the Executive Guideline Steering Group (Executive GSG), the WHO Steering Group, the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the External Review Group, and the systematic review team and guideline methodologists. The Executive GSG, an independent panel of external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions, advised WHO on prioritizing new and existing questions in maternal and perinatal health for recommendation development or updating. The WHO Steering Group, comprising WHO staff from the Departments of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), managed the updating process. This group supervised evidence retrieval and synthesis, organized the GDG meeting, and managed the dissemination, implementation, and impact assessment of the guideline. The GDG consisted of 14 external experts and stakeholders with expertise in PPH research, guideline development methods, and clinical policy and programs related to PPH prevention and treatment. The group appraised the evidence, advised on its interpretation, formulated the final recommendation, and reviewed and approved the final document. The GDG ensured geographic representation and gender balance, with no significant conflicts of interest. The External Review Group included five technical experts who reviewed the final document for factual errors, clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. They ensured that the decision-making process incorporated the contextual values and preferences of potential users of the recommendations, healthcare professionals, and policymakers. A Cochrane systematic review on TXA use for PPH treatment was initiated and supported by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. The WHO Steering Group reviewed and provided input into the protocol and worked closely with the Cochrane Group to appraise the evidence using the GRADE methodology. Evidence profiles summarizing the effects of TXA on prespecified outcomes were prepared, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The quality of evidence for each outcome was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on established criteria, including study design limitations, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The GDG used these evidence profiles to formulate the updated recommendation, which was reviewed and approved during an online technical consultation organized by the Steering Group.
